answer: Run hours are derived from each equipment's binary status point (e.g. AHU 'Un-SAF/St' supply-fan status, chiller 'CH-St', pump '*-St') by integrating the time the signal = 1 over the last 7 complete days (2026-06-20 00:00 to 2026-06-27 00:00 Australia/Sydney). 99 Elizabeth St has ~316 equipment / 397 status points; a full-site figure is NOT computable within the 30-call / response-size budget because each status point alone returns ~672 weekly COV samples and gets truncated at 672 rows (losing ~24h at the window end). For the central chillers, computed accurately: CH-01 ~11.7 run hours (brief overnight cooling cycles), CH-02 0 run hours (off all week). To complete the rest, run one platform.history call per status fav_id (or small fav_id batches with start/end windowing to dodge the row cap) and sum the on-time the same way.

wall_notes: Site resolution and equipment/status discovery were clean. The blocker is data volume: run hours require integrating raw binary status timeseries, and every single-point weekly query returns ~672 COV samples that hit the response-size cap (truncated at exactly 672 rows, cutting ~24h off the window end). With 316 equipment / 397 status points, fetching weekly history for even the ~40 real run-hours assets (chillers, pumps, CTs, 28 AHU fans) would need ~40 separate calls (batching via fav_ids only compounds rows and truncates), exceeding the 30-call budget. There is no server-side run-hours/aggregation field - platform.history only returns raw data+ts. I scoped down to the two central chillers and computed those exactly (CH-01 11.69h, CH-02 0h). I did pull two full ~672-row raw series into context to validate the integration method and confirm the truncation behaviour; for a production report you would window each point and aggregate locally rather than ingest raw rows.
